content: Based on case reports, individuals with a history of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) may have an increased risk of developing thrombocytopenia, particularly if they experienced thrombocytopenic purpura after a prior dose of the MMR vaccine. Revaccination Risks There is no evidence to suggest an increased risk of adverse reactions when live measles vaccines are administered to individuals who are already immune to measles, either due to prior vaccination or natural infection. Precautions and Contraindications Pregnancy: Live measles vaccines, whether as part of the MR or MMR vaccine, should not be administered to women who are known to be pregnant or planning to become pregnant within the next three months. Women who receive the monovalent measles vaccine should avoid becoming pregnant for at least 30 days post-vaccination. This precaution is based on a theoretical risk of fetal infection, although no evidence currently supports this risk. To protect adolescents and young adults from measles, it is sufficient to ask women if they are pregnant, exclude those who are, and explain the theoretical risks to others before vaccination. Febrile Illness: The decision to vaccinate or delay vaccination in the presence of a current or recent febrile illness depends on the cause and severity of the illness. Minor illnesses, such as mild upper respiratory infections with or without low-grade fever, are not contraindications for vaccination. For individuals with uncertain compliance to medical care, every opportunity should be taken to administer appropriate vaccinations. Children with moderate or severe febrile illnesses can be vaccinated once they have recovered from the acute phase of the illness. This approach avoids overlapping adverse effects of vaccination with the underlying illness or misattributing symptoms of the illness to the vaccine. Routine physical examinations or temperature measurements are not prerequisites for vaccinating infants and children who appear healthy. Asking parents or guardians if the child is ill, postponing vaccination for those with moderate or severe febrile illnesses, and vaccinating those without contraindications are appropriate practices in childhood immunization programs. Allergic Reactions Hypersensitivity reactions following MMR or its component vaccines are rare. Most reactions are mild, presenting as localized wheal-and-flare or urticaria at the injection site. Immediate anaphylactic reactions to MMR or its components are extremely rare. Despite the distribution of over 70 million doses of MMR vaccine in the United States since the implementation of VAERS in 1990, only 33 cases of anaphylactic reactions post-MMR vaccination have been reported. Of these, only 11 cases occurred immediately after vaccination and were consistent with anaphylaxis. Historically, individuals with severe allergic reactions (e.g., hives, mouth or throat swelling, difficulty breathing, hypotension, or shock) following egg ingestion were considered at increased risk for serious reactions to measles-containing vaccines, which are produced in chick embryo fibroblasts. Protocols involving skin testing and cautious vaccination were developed for such individuals. However, recent studies suggest that anaphylactic reactions to measles-containing vaccines are not associated with hypersensitivity to egg antigens but rather to other vaccine components. The risk of serious allergic reactions to these vaccines in egg-allergic individuals is extremely low, and skin testing is not necessarily predictive of vaccine hypersensitivity. Consequently, ACIP is reevaluating the necessity of skin testing and special protocols for vaccinating egg-allergic individuals with measles-containing vaccines. MMR and its component vaccines contain hydrolyzed gelatin as a stabilizer. There is a documented case of an individual with anaphylactic sensitivity to gelatin who experienced an anaphylactic reaction after receiving the MMR vaccine licensed in the United States. Similar cases have been reported in Japan. ACIP is currently considering recommendations for vaccinating individuals with a history of anaphylactic reactions to gelatin or gelatin-containing products. In the meantime, such individuals should be vaccinated with MMR and its components with extreme caution. MMR vaccines also contain trace amounts of neomycin. Although the amount is less than that used in skin tests for hypersensitivity, individuals with a history of anaphylactic reactions to neomycin should not receive these vaccines. Most neomycin allergies manifest as contact dermatitis rather than anaphylaxis. A history of contact dermatitis to neomycin is not a contraindication to receiving measles vaccines. Additionally, live measles virus vaccines do not contain penicillin.
